Metadata.title: Haithem Mustafa · Full Stack Engineer
Metadata.description: Full stack engineer in Baghdad, backend first. I build software people in Iraq use every day: a bank's internal workflows, a hospital system, a ride-hailing backend and an AI that answers customer chats.

Hero.intro: I build software that people in Iraq use every day: a bank's paperwork, a hospital's emergency room, a ride-hailing app, and an AI that answers shops' customer chats.
Hero.subtitle: Now at Asia Al-Iraq Islamic Bank · Co-founder of Rdood

About.title: A bit about me.
paragraphs: I'm Haithem, a software engineer from Baghdad. I studied Computer Engineering at the University of Technology, and I've been building for the web since 2022.

Most of my time goes into the backend: the servers, databases and background jobs that keep an app working when lots of people use it at once. I write them in TypeScript or Rust, almost always on PostgreSQL. I build the screens too, and I usually end up running the Linux servers it all lives on.

Today I work at Asia Al-Iraq Islamic Bank, where I build the bank's internal systems and look after its servers, network and email. Outside the bank, I co-founded Rdood, and I still take on freelance projects.

Projects.title: Things I've built.
Projects.subtitle: Six I'd show you first, then everything else, newest first.
Projects.allSubtitle: Every project, newest first. Each one has a short story: what it is, who uses it, what I built and what was hard.

wfis.name: WFIS
wfis.tagline: The bank's paper forms, moved online
wfis.status: Live on the bank's own network
wfis.summary: WFIS replaced the paper request forms at Asia Al-Iraq Islamic Bank. A request no longer travels from desk to desk on paper: it follows the bank's own org chart from person to person, gets approved and signed, and ends up in an archive nobody can quietly change. I built it, and I run the servers it lives on.
wfis.users: Bank staff raise requests at their desks, managers approve them from their phones, and administrators and auditors set it up and check the records.
built: 27 of the bank's forms, each printed on the bank's own document layout, in Arabic first with a full English version.
Routing that follows the real org chart, including deputies, delegations and people acting in someone else's seat. Admins change it on screen, not in code.
Signatures that ask for a fresh code from an authenticator app, and an audit trail that shows if anything was altered.
Phone apps for Android and iPhone with push notifications and a document scanner, so managers can approve on the move.
Two servers in a failover pair, with tested backups and written restore steps.
wfis.hard: Making a form look exactly the same on screen and on paper, in Arabic. Printed forms kept coming out with the wrong typeface or an extra second page, and it looked like a data bug. It wasn't. The bank's template asks for Arial, the server had no Arial and quietly swapped in another font, and Word and LibreOffice disagreed about where a page ends. So I stopped guessing and measured the rendered PDF: which fonts it embedded, where each character landed and how many pages it had. Measuring is what found the real causes.

numbers.label: for the standby server to take over when we cut the power

rdood.name: Rdood
rdood.tagline: An AI that answers shops' customer chats, in Iraqi Arabic
rdood.status: Live, used by shops in Iraq
rdood.summary: Rdood (ردود, Arabic for "replies") gives online shops in Iraq one inbox for WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger and Telegram. Its AI agent answers customers in Iraqi Arabic, takes orders and follows up, and the shop's staff can step in whenever they like. I co-founded it and lead the engineering.
rdood.users: Shop staff answer and watch chats from their phones, owners set the agent up on a computer, and partners can manage several shops at once.
built: Rdood's own AI agent, built in-house: it looks things up and takes actions through tools, and anything that touches money waits for a person to approve it.
Orders, follow-ups, delivery through local couriers, and WhatsApp campaigns sent through approved templates.
Voice notes turned into text, and WhatsApp calls the AI can answer.
Staff apps for Android and iPhone, and a web app for everything else.
The Arabic-first marketing site, rdoodplatform.com.
rdood.hard: Knowing what the AI costs. Every answer the agent writes costs money, and that money has to land on the right shop's bill. When I checked our development data, about two thirds of the real spend wasn't being recorded at all: eight different places in the code called the AI, and only some of them wrote the cost down. Instead of patching eight places, I moved the metering into the one client every call goes through. Now a call can't happen without knowing which shop it's for, and if writing the bill fails, the customer still gets their reply.
shots: Rdood's home page, Arabic first, for shop owners in Iraq.
The demo on the home page: the AI agent takes an order in Iraqi Arabic and confirms it.
The same page on a phone.

lst.name: LST Hospital System
lst.tagline: A hospital system built around the emergency room
lst.summary: LST is a healthcare provider in Erbil, and this is the system its staff work in. A patient arrives, gets triaged and queued, sees a doctor, gets tests, medicine and a bed if needed, and the bill and the insurance claim are built from what actually happened. It works in Arabic and English, and every role gets the screens its job needs.
lst.users: Reception, doctors, nurses, lab and radiology staff, pharmacists, cashiers and warehouse staff, each with their own screens and permissions.
built: The emergency room first: triage, patient queues and live boards that show who is waiting and where.
Admissions and beds, lab, radiology, physiotherapy, ambulance trips and home-care visits, all hanging off one shared patient visit.
The pharmacy and chronic prescriptions, tied to the warehouse stock.
Billing on a ledger (invoices, payments, refunds) and insurance: policies, coverage rules, pre-approvals and claims.
Arabic and English, a role for every job, and an audit log of who did what.
lst.hard: Money and medicine can't be wrong. The stock ledger only ever grows, so a bad movement stays in the books for good, and a double click must never sell the same box twice. So money is kept in whole Iraqi dinars, ledgers can't be edited, and every money or stock write carries a key that makes a repeat harmless. Stock moves inside one database transaction under a lock, and always takes the batch that expires first.
shots: The executive overview: admissions, bed occupancy, insurance claims and low stock on one screen. Demo data.
A patient arrives at the ER: find or register them, note the complaint and set a triage level from 1 to 5.
The warehouse: what is in stock, what has run out and what needs reordering. Demo data.
Users and roles: 19 staff roles, and a grid of what each one is allowed to do.

tan.name: TAN
tan.tagline: A car marketplace built around short videos
tan.summary: TAN is an app where people in Iraq buy and sell cars, and show them off in short videos. I built the whole backend: listings, the video feed, chat, payments and everything that runs in the background. More than 30,000 people have signed up.
tan.users: Car buyers and sellers across Iraq. Dealers pay to promote their listings and to get a verified badge.
built: The video pipeline: phones upload straight to storage in parts, then a separate worker turns each clip into 360p, 720p and 1080p streams served through a CDN.
Chat and notifications in real time, with end-to-end encrypted direct messages.
The feed: likes, comments, follows, trending hashtags and a ranking that updates in the background.
QiCard payments for promoted listings and verified badges, with renewals and refunds.
Search across people, cars and videos in Arabic and English, plus the reports and appeals moderators need.
tan.hard: Video. Turning a phone clip into streams for every connection speed takes real processing power, and if that work ran inside the API, everyone's app would slow down while one video converted. So uploads go from the phone straight to storage, never through the API, and a separate worker converts each video once, in one pass, then hands the finished stream to the CDN. When a job fails, the worker knows whether to retry or give up, so one broken file can't block the queue.
shots: The admin's listings table: every car for sale, its price, status and views. Demo data.
Moderating the short videos people post about their cars.
The admin dashboard: users, listings, videos, payments and open reports at a glance.

beeb.name: Beeb
beeb.tagline: Ride-hailing and parcel delivery for Baghdad
beeb.summary: Beeb is a ride-hailing and parcel delivery app for Baghdad. I wrote its server: the part that prices your trip, finds a driver near you and keeps both phones in sync while the car moves. More than 2,100 drivers have signed up.
beeb.users: Riders who book trips and send parcels, drivers who take them, and the operations team who watch it all from an admin dashboard.
built: Driver matching on a real map: the city is split into zones, and each request goes to nearby drivers in the right zone.
Our own routing server, so trip distances and times come from Baghdad's actual roads.
Live trips: rider and driver see each other's status and position as it changes.
Fares by distance, time and zone, scheduled trips with several stops, and a wallet for card and cash.
Driver sign-up with document checks, and parcel delivery on the same system.
beeb.hard: Keeping two phones in agreement while a car moves through traffic. Every trip has a rider and a driver, each holding a live connection to the server, and those two connections can land on different server processes. I put Redis in the middle: each update is published once and reaches whichever process holds the other phone. So the rider watches the driver move, and a cancelled trip is cancelled on both screens at once.

news-auditor.name: AI News Auditor
news-auditor.tagline: Watches Iraqi TV news around the clock and flags what breaks the rules
news-auditor.summary: AI News Auditor watches and listens to six Iraqi news channels day and night. It writes down what's said, reads the text on screen, recognises faces and voices, and checks every minute against a set of broadcast rules. When something might break a rule, it goes into a short queue for a person to decide, with the evidence attached: the clip, the quoted words and the rule.
news-auditor.users: Reviewers who decide each case, supervisors and editors who manage the rules and the people database, and viewers who follow the results.
built: Recording and live speech-to-text for six channels, around the clock, on models we run ourselves.
Reading on-screen text in Arabic, and matching faces and voices against a database of people.
A rule engine: simple rules are checked in code, and judgement calls get a quick AI screen, then a stricter check that has to quote its evidence.
Alerts when a channel goes black, freezes, goes silent or loses its signal, and spotting adverts.
An Arabic, right-to-left app for reviewers: a case queue, search and a wall of live channels.
news-auditor.hard: Keeping the text in step with the picture. At first the transcript landed anywhere from 41 seconds to almost 7 minutes behind the broadcast, and a channel that fell behind never caught up. I timed every stage and found several small causes instead of one big one: the speech engine was busy with other work, the audio sent to it was heavier than it needed to be, and fixed waits were built into the loop. Smaller audio, overlapping windows (the next piece goes out while the last one is still being read) and a faster machine as the main engine brought it down to 9 to 16 seconds behind live.

numbers.label: behind live, down from up to 7 minutes

lussano.name: Lussano Piano Center
lussano.tagline: A piano academy's website, lessons, bookings and shop in one system
lussano.summary: Lussano is a piano academy in Baghdad. I'm building the one system that replaces its WordPress site: the website, a course platform with video lessons, bookings, check-ins at the academy, a shop, and an admin the staff can run from their phones.
lussano.users: Students (parents make an account for each child), visitors, and staff: teachers, the front desk, editors, the shop and the owner.
built: Video lessons by level and chapter, opened by a subscription, a purchase, a trial or a gift.
Check-ins at the academy by QR code and GPS: a counted visit unlocks the next chapter.
Booking with fees, and a shop with delivery fees per governorate, paid through Wayl or in cash.
The website, with the carved plaster wall that gave this site its background.
An admin for all of it, with audit logs, and an authenticator app required for every staff sign-in.
lussano.hard: Catching whoever leaks a lesson. Each lesson is encoded in two versions that differ in ways you can't see, and every account gets its own mix of the two, chosen by a secret key. Give the tool a leaked recording and it reads the mix back, ranks the accounts it could have come from, and says how likely the match is to be luck. It's honest about its limits too: a still screenshot or a very short clip can't be traced.
shots: Lussano's home page, with the carved plaster wall that rises under the cursor.
Three ways to learn: at the academy, the online course, and lessons for children.
The same page on a phone.

iraqview.name: IraqView
iraqview.tagline: Order design and marketing work, and get a smart business card
iraqview.summary: IraqView is where people and small businesses in Iraq order design, branding and marketing work, and buy a Smart Digital Card: a profile page with a tap-to-share NFC card. I led the team of three that built it, in Arabic, English and Kurdish, with prices in dinars and dollars.
iraqview.users: Customers ordering work and cards, the designers who deliver it, and the admins who run prices, limits and page copy.
built: An order flow with nine steps from request to delivery, with chat, files, revisions and payment in stages on every order.
The Smart Card: a public profile page for each person, subscriptions, and a printed NFC card on yearly plans.
Arabic, English and Kurdish (Sorani), in dinars and dollars, with the exchange rate saved on every payment.
An admin panel where prices, limits and page copy are data, not code.
Two-factor sign-in, nightly backups and a restore drill.
iraqview.hard: A green test suite isn't proof. Ours passed, so I broke the code on purpose to see whether the tests would notice (mutation testing). Too often they didn't: it turned up a finished order that could still be cancelled, and an invoice test that compared the invoice with itself. Both were fixed, and the tests now prove what they claim. QA also caught three quick clicks on Pay charging one instalment three times, before it ever reached a customer.
shots: IraqView's home page: design, branding and marketing orders in one place, followed step by step.
The same page on a phone.

heidi.name: Heidi Mind Care
heidi.tagline: Online booking for a UK therapy practice
heidi.summary: Heidi Mind Care is a therapy practice in the UK. I built its website: clients read about the services, pick a real open time and book, and the practice runs clients, notes, appointments and the blog from its own admin. It works in English and Arabic.
heidi.users: The practice's clients, and the practice itself through the admin.
built: A booking flow that shows only real open times, in London time and in the visitor's own.
Payment through Stripe, confirmation emails, and cancellation by the client.
An admin for client records, notes, enquiries, availability and manual bookings.
Service pages, a blog and an FAQ the practice edits itself.
English and Arabic, with pages search engines can read and proper share previews.
heidi.hard: Two people must never book the same hour. Open times are worked out from availability rules rather than stored, so there's no row to lock. When someone starts booking, a 12-minute hold is saved, and the database itself refuses a second hold on the same time. Unpaid holds are released by a background job, a booking is confirmed only when Stripe's payment notice arrives and checks out, and every payment request carries a key, so a retry never charges twice.
shots: The home page: calm colours and one clear next step, booking a session.
The same page on a phone.

numbers.label: hold on a time while you pay

netaudit.name: NetAudit
netaudit.tagline: A desktop app that reads a network and shows what's wrong with it
netaudit.status: In use inside the bank, still growing
netaudit.summary: NetAudit helps the bank's IT team understand their own network. It reads each device's configuration, draws the network as a diagram, points out problems with the evidence behind each one, and answers "what if" questions: where a packet would go, what can reach what, and what breaks if a link goes down. Reports come out in Arabic and English.
netaudit.users: The bank's IT and network staff, with managers and auditors reading the reports.
built: Importers that turn device configurations and survey files into one model of the network.
A topology diagram drawn from that model.
An issue finder that shows the evidence behind every finding.
A simulator: packet traces, a reachability matrix, and link-failure checks that find single points of failure.
Reports in Arabic and English (PDF, Excel and HTML), in a desktop app for Windows and Linux.
netaudit.hard: A tool like this is dangerous if it shows a guess as a fact. So every result says how sure it is: confirmed when two independent sources agree, likely when only one does, and unverified when data is missing. Wherever the model predicts something a device can report about itself, NetAudit compares the two, and a mismatch becomes an issue of its own and lowers trust in that part of the model.

numbers.label: levels of certainty on every result

asiabank.name: asiabank.iq
asiabank.tagline: The bank's public website, rebuilt from WordPress
asiabank.summary: I rebuilt the bank's public website from WordPress into a fast site made of plain pages, in Arabic and English. Every old address still works, and the bank's staff can change any text or image themselves: they click it on the real page, edit it and press Publish.
asiabank.users: Customers and investors reading about the bank, and staff keeping the site up to date.
built: The whole site, rebuilt with Astro on Cloudflare, with every old WordPress address kept or redirected.
A new design for the whole site, built around the bank's logo.
112 document pages (policies, charters and reports) and designed pages for the home page, investors, the Sharia board and services.
A visual editor: click text or an image on the live page, change it, publish.
Editor sign-in with an authenticator app, recovery codes and a sign-in history.
Contact, newsletter and whistleblowing forms that work even without JavaScript, with spam protection.
asiabank.hard: Letting staff edit a site that is just files. The editor never touches the source. Each edit remembers what its element held, its text or link and its place among similar elements, and when someone presses Publish the site is rebuilt with the edits written in. If a later code change means an edit no longer matches anything, it's flagged and skipped, so it can never land on the wrong part of a page.
shots: The bank's public website, in Arabic and English.
The same page on a phone.

ar-card.name: AR business card
ar-card.tagline: Point your phone at a business card, and a video plays on it
ar-card.summary: Point a phone camera at a printed business card and a video appears on it, stuck to the card as if it were printed there, even as you move. There's no app to install: it all runs in the browser. I wrote the tracking myself, in Rust compiled to WebAssembly.
ar-card.users: Built for a client of The Studio, to bring their printed cards to life.
built: A computer-vision tracker in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly with SIMD so it runs fast in a phone's browser.
Finding the card from corner features (FAST and BRIEF), matched with RANSAC.
Following the card from frame to frame with optical flow.
Anchoring against the original card image to stop the video drifting.
A WebGL2 video overlay, with the QR code as a fallback.
ar-card.hard: Following a dark, glossy card in a moving hand, in real time, in a browser. Optical flow follows the card from one frame to the next, but small errors add up and the video slowly slides off. The fix compares small patches of the live picture with the original card image and pulls the tracking back into place, in a way that copes with glare sliding across the card.

alhikma.name: Alhikma Akademie
alhikma.tagline: An online school for Arabic and the Quran
alhikma.summary: Alhikma Akademie teaches Arabic and the Quran online. I built the platform its students learn on (courses, exercises, live chat with teachers, video lessons and video calls) and the back office the school runs on. I also look after its production server.
alhikma.users: Students on paid subscriptions, their teachers, and the school's admins and moderators.
built: Courses at several levels, with listening, reading, writing and speaking exercises.
Quran memorization that brings each surah back for review on a spaced-repetition schedule.
Vocabulary study with example sentences and an Arabic dictionary.
Live chat with moderation, and scheduled video calls with teachers.
Video lessons: upload, conversion and streaming.
alhikma.hard: Moving a live school off WordPress. The platform started as a set of custom WordPress plugins on MySQL, and students were using it every day, so it couldn't stop while it was rebuilt. I moved it to a new Fastify and PostgreSQL backend one module at a time: the newsletter first, then reviews, chat, courses, videos, the Quran tracker and the rest. The course module, the biggest of them, ran on both databases while its data moved across.
shots: Al-Hikma Akademie's home page, in German, for learning the Quran and Arabic online.
The same page on a phone.

studio-platform.name: The Studio platform
studio-platform.tagline: The system a creative agency runs on, with a portal for its clients
studio-platform.status: In use; the client portal is live
studio-platform.summary: The Studio is a creative agency, and this is the system it runs on: clients and the sales pipeline, HR, tasks, a shared mailbox and admin, in English, French and Arabic. The agency's clients get their own portal, where they request work and follow it as it moves.
studio-platform.users: The agency's team, across 12 roles that each see what they need, and its clients, through the portal.
built: A sales pipeline with follow-ups, Google Calendar sync, and CSV import that catches duplicates.
A shared mailbox on IMAP where new mail shows up live.
Tasks on Kanban boards, with approvals.
HR: time off and overtime, with approvals in several steps.
The client portal: clients pick services, send requests and watch each one move from pending to done, with notes going both ways.
studio-platform.hard: Two kinds of people on one system. Staff and clients sign in to different apps that share the same data, and staff often need to be signed in to both at once, to see what a client sees. So the portal has its own sign-in, separate from the staff one, and both sessions live side by side. Every change a client should see is pushed to them live, on that request's own channel.

torch.name: Torch Business OS
torch.tagline: One system to run a company, from payroll to email
torch.summary: TORCH was building one system for running a company: HR and payroll, email, documents, sign-in and more, opened from a single desktop app. I led the backend team and built much of the core: about 20 small services that talk through a shared event bus, plus the desktop app that ties them together.
torch.users: A company's staff: HR teams running payroll and attendance, and everyone else reading email, handling documents and signing in once for everything.
built: One sign-in for everything: an identity service with two-factor, passkeys and single sign-on (SAML and OpenID).
HR: payroll, attendance and leave, reading clock-ins straight from fingerprint devices.
Email as its own service, with new mail pushed to the inbox as it arrives.
A desktop app (Tauri, Rust and React) that installs and updates the other apps, signs you in once and shares that sign-in with each of them.
Tracing and metrics across every service, so a slow request can be followed from start to finish.
torch.hard: Twenty services that mustn't call each other directly. If HR calls Email, which calls Notifications, one slow service drags the rest down with it. Instead, each service announces what happened on a shared Redis event bus (a user signed in, a domain was verified) and the services that care react in their own time. Shared packages keep the shape of every event the same everywhere, so one service can change without breaking the others.

numbers.label: systems for the desktop app: Linux, Windows and macOS

alshabaka.name: Alshabaka
alshabaka.tagline: A streaming service for films, series and live TV
alshabaka.summary: Alshabaka streams films, series, live TV, theatre and music. I took over its backend from another team, made it faster, and kept shipping new features.
alshabaka.users: Viewers on the web, on their phones and on smart TVs.
built: Sped up the API and shipped new features on a system that was already live.
Watch history that follows viewers between their devices in real time.
Sign-in on a TV by scanning a QR code with your phone.
Search across the catalogue, with Elasticsearch and events through Kafka.
Streaming over HLS, with access by subscription and filtering by age rating.
alshabaka.hard: Taking over a big system that was already live. Alshabaka had more than 50 modules and viewers on it every day when it came to me, so every fix had to ship without breaking what already worked.
shots: Browsing as a guest: series, films, live channels and music in one catalogue.
Signing in on a phone, with a phone number or an email.

studio-website.name: The Studio website
studio-website.tagline: A creative agency's own website, in English and Arabic
studio-website.summary: The Studio's website: a 3D logo, a particle field and animation that follows your scroll, in English and Arabic.
studio-website.users: People looking for an agency, and the agency's team showing off its work.
built: A 3D logo and particle field with Three.js, whose colours change from section to section.
Scroll-driven reveals with GSAP, and smooth scrolling with Lenis.
English and Arabic, right to left included.
Home, services, work and a page for every case study.
Light and dark themes, and a contact form.
studio-website.hard: A lot moves on this site: a 3D logo, a particle field and scroll animation, in two languages and two directions. To keep the first load quick, every page and every language loads only when it's needed.
shots: The first view of The Studio's website.
The same page on a phone.

alseraj.name: Alseraj website
alseraj.tagline: A company website, from design to launch
alseraj.summary: Alseraj's company website. I did all of it: the design, the build, the words on the pages and the launch, and I kept it running afterwards.
alseraj.users: Alseraj's customers, and anyone searching for what it does.
built: A fast website built with Next.js that can be installed like an app and loads quickly on phones.
Search basics done properly: page structure, meta tags and speed.
Page animations and smooth scrolling.
The copy and the layout of every page.
Launch with monitoring and automatic deploys.
